title: Troubleshooting Peak Shape Problems in HPLC
evidence: Peak-shape changes can arise from the HPLC system, mobile phase, sample, or column. A high-value first distinction is whether all peaks are affected or only selected analytes. Waters also presents a guard-column example in which replacing the fouled guard restored peak symmetry, illustrating how a targeted intervention can confirm involvement of that component.
guardrail: Do not infer that a guard column or column is the cause merely because peak shape changed; isolate the component and confirm the predicted response.

title: Peak Shape Changes for a Previously Used Column
evidence: When a previously acceptable column gives changed peak symmetry, comparing pressure, retention time, peak area, peak width, and symmetry can help localize the problem. In the Waters example, reseating a poor column connection restored tailing factors, confirming extra-column dead volume from the connection.
guardrail: A connection problem is only one hypothesis; confirmation requires an isolated reconnection/reseating test and recovery of the affected metric.

title: My Chromatography Has Changed: Steps for Effective Troubleshooting
evidence: Agilent organizes changed chromatography into symptom groups including pressure, peak shape, retention/resolution, and baseline. This supports symptom-first localization rather than jumping directly to a component replacement.
guardrail: Use the symptom grouping to structure investigation, not as proof of a specific root cause.

title: LC Troubleshooting Tips
evidence: Shimadzu lists several distinct high-pressure mechanisms, including excessive flow setting, column blockage, incompatible/precipitated mobile phase, incorrect column characteristics, and injector blockage. These possibilities should be separated with location-specific tests instead of treated as interchangeable causes.
guardrail: Do not backflush or replace a column unless the column manufacturer and laboratory procedure permit it and evidence localizes the restriction there.

title: Chromatography Troubleshooting Guides — Liquid Chromatography
evidence: Thermo Fisher identifies several separable causes of varying retention, including inadequate equilibration, leaks, temperature fluctuation, column contamination, solvent-reservoir restrictions, incorrect pump mixing, dwell-volume differences, leaking piston seals, and air in solvent lines. These should be discriminated using the case pattern and targeted checks.
guardrail: A retention shift alone does not identify which mechanism is responsible; compare what changed and use one discriminating test at a time.

title: Can air bubbles in the mobile phase affect chromatography?
evidence: Waters notes that air bubbles can affect multiple chromatographic responses, including peak area, peak shape, retention time, baseline noise, and back pressure.
guardrail: Because air can produce multiple symptoms, verify direct evidence of air/flow-delivery instability before attributing the problem to bubbles.

title: Peak Area Precision
evidence: Thermo Fisher lists contamination/carryover, autosampler needle or needle-seat issues, unstable environmental conditions, and improper capillary connections/dead volume among possible contributors to poor peak-area precision.
guardrail: Poor area precision is a symptom; distinguish random/sequential behavior and common-mode versus analyte-specific effects before selecting a component test.

title: Solving Carryover Problems in HPLC
evidence: Shimadzu distinguishes classic carryover that decreases across successive blanks from constant contamination that does not behave like true carryover. Varying blank injection volume and observing how the suspect peak responds can help distinguish blank contamination from external-needle or internal needle/loop sources.
guardrail: Do not label every blank peak as carryover; first classify its behavior and exclude contamination of the blank itself.

title: Ghost Peaks
evidence: Thermo Fisher lists contamination, commonly in the injector or column, as one cause of ghost peaks and also notes detector-setting causes such as reference wavelength or bandwidth. This supports separating chemical contamination from detector/acquisition explanations.
guardrail: A ghost peak is not proof of injector contamination; isolate with blanks and component-specific checks.

title: HILIC Column Troubleshooting Guide — Baseline and Contamination Principles
evidence: Thermo Fisher recommends distinguishing baseline problems with a blank and notes that mobile-phase contamination can contribute to background, spikes, and noise. Detector warm-up and column equilibration are also relevant checks.
guardrail: Use blank behavior to localize the source; do not assume the column or detector without comparative evidence.

title: USP <621> Chromatography
evidence: USP <621> provides general chromatographic procedures, definitions, calculations, and system-suitability requirements. The applicable monograph/procedure remains the controlling source for method-specific acceptance criteria and permitted adjustments.
guardrail: Do not invent a USP limit or permitted adjustment. Verify the applicable current chapter/monograph and local approved procedure before changing method conditions.

title: Investigating Out-of-Specification (OOS) Test Results for Pharmaceutical Production
evidence: FDA guidance requires scientifically sound investigation of OOS results and documentation of the assessment. Retesting should not substitute for investigation or be used simply to obtain a passing result; conclusions that assign laboratory error require supporting evidence.
guardrail: The app provides decision support only; formal OOS/OOT handling must follow the laboratory's approved SOP, QA oversight, applicable regulations, and the current guidance.

title: ICH Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures and Q14 Analytical Procedure Development
evidence: ICH Q2(R2) and Q14 frame analytical procedures across development, validation, and lifecycle management. Changes should be evaluated scientifically and with risk-based consideration of which performance characteristics may be affected and whether partial or full revalidation is needed.
guardrail: Do not treat troubleshooting adjustments as automatically validated method changes; distinguish diagnostic testing from approved routine method conditions.

title: Diagnosing HPLC Chromatography Problems & Troubleshooting
evidence: Shimadzu illustrates how the pattern of which metrics change can help localize a problem: for example, retention-time shifts with stable area can point toward flow-delivery issues, while peak-height change with stable area and retention can indicate a different mechanism. Pattern comparison is more informative than a single symptom alone.
guardrail: Vendor examples are diagnostic patterns, not universal proof. Confirm with measurements on the actual system.
